title: St. Louis on the St. Paul: first Black band for white audiences
summary: In 1919 they played nightly on the St. Paul, the first time Black bands played for whites in St. Louis, with guards protecting them and hostility from white musicians.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Yeah, I'm going to stop drinking. But then we get back to the boat. To the boat. We played every night in St. Louis on the steamer St. Paul. And on a Saturday was a matinee at 2 o'clock. See? No, I'm here to my time. This changed. When we first went there in 1919, we played from 9 o'clock in the morning to 11 o'clock at night. What? Yeah. See? But after we went back there the next year, then we played just night. From 9 on to 11 o'clock at night and nobody, man, we played and it was fun. See? And that's the first time that Negroes ever played for the White in St. Louis. Oh yeah? Yeah. See? Because before 1919, there were Negro bands around St. Louis, but they only played colored parties. There were no big bands. And we had guards, we had the gangsters, gardeners from the boat up the river. And I didn't know there was gardeners. I didn't know it. I didn't know it until we got through. Gardening for what? The White in the system won't understand. It was Streck. Oh yeah? Yeah. So Streck was just high a lot of guards. Take you up the hill. Oh, I see. Take you up the hill and bring you down the hill. See? At the foot of the Washington River, you know, when that water is low, it's a steep hill you go down, right down to the river. Take you up the hill where? Where you was staying? No, take you up the hill to let you catch the street after you get on the car. Then you was all right. See? Because you had to walk way up the hill right by the Washington River, you know, before you go across the East Bridge. Uh-huh. Where you got about seven or eight blocks. Yeah. Right down that hill to go down that river. See? And I thought, see, well, it used to wash it. But nobody worried us. But the White musicians was hard on us. Where did you live then? St. Louis then? I stayed in St. Louis for four months. We was up there for four months.
